title: Logarithms: Visual Guide
outline: 1. Undoing The Exponential | b^x and log_b(x) drawn together with the line y = x, a base picker and an exponent slider that moves one point on each curve with its coordinates swapped | a logarithm is the exponential run backwards, so the same fact is the point (exponent, value) on one curve and (value, exponent) on the other, which is where the domain x > 0, the range of every real, and the two cancellation identities all come from

2. Same Three Numbers | the base and exponent dragged while the exponential form and the logarithmic form update side by side, with the wrong-slot permutations priced out underneath | log_b(a) = c and b^c = a are one claim about a base, an exponent and a result, so every distractor in this topic is those three numbers dropped into someone else's slot

3. Three Laws One Source | product, quotient, power and the fake log(x + y) rule, each evaluated on both sides at the numbers you choose, with the two-line derivation from the exponent properties beneath | every logarithm law is an exponent law read backwards, so a product inside becomes a sum outside and a power becomes a coefficient — and log(x + y) has no rule because no exponent property covers a sum of powers

4. Change Of Base | log_b(x) computed by the natural-log route and the common-log route at once, bracketed between the neighbouring integer powers, with the three formulas it gets confused with | change of base evaluates a logarithm in any base from the two keys a calculator actually has, and it is a ratio with the target on top and the old base underneath — never a difference, never inverted, never a log of a quotient

5. Constant Ratio | initial value and percentage rate dragged into A(t) = A0(1 + r)^t, with bars, a table of differences against ratios, and the doubling time solved by logarithms | percentage change compounds, so the growth factor is 1 + r and the signature in a table is a constant ratio over equal intervals, not a constant difference — and once t is stuck in the exponent only a logarithm brings it down
